label: Reading
text: Basic Skills

label: Reading
text: Understanding question constraints

label: Reading
text: Pay close attention to the specific instructions in the question. They dictate exactly how you should provide your answer. Before you read the passage, scan the question for these keywords:

label: Reading
text: Quantity: Are you asked to write ONE word, TWO words, or NO MORE THAN THREE words? Exceeding the word limit will result in a loss of marks.

label: Reading
text: Form: Does the question ask for a 'word' or a 'phrase'? A phrase is a group of words. Make sure your answer matches the required grammatical form. If it asks for a word, extracting a phrase will not be accepted.

label: Reading
text: Target Paragraph: Look for instructions like "taken from paragraphs 6 to 7". You must locate the answer only within these specified paragraphs. An answer from elsewhere, even if it contains the correct information, will not score marks.

label: Reading
text: Grammar: Pay attention to phrases like "Your answers must be grammatically correct." If the question states "taken from the passage", you usually need to copy the exact word. However, sometimes a word needs to change from singular to plural or verb tense to fit the new sentence. Always read the context carefully.

label: Reading
text: Skimming

label: Reading
text: To understand the topic of a text, you do not need to read every word. Skimming is useful when answering questions that require you to identify the theme or overall views expressed in a text.

label: Reading
text: Look at the title, the subtitles as well as the first and last paragraphs.

label: Reading
text: Read the first and last sentences of the other paragraphs.

label: Reading
text: Think about the overall meaning of the text.

label: Reading
text: Thematic questions

label: Reading
text: A thematic question is about the overall theme of a text (what the whole text is about). A thematic question may ask you:

label: Reading
text: about the writer's main message or conclusion

label: Reading
text: to choose an alternative title for the text

label: Reading
text: to identify the type of text or the target audience

label: Reading
text: to identify the source of the text

label: Reading
text: The last 3 points are mostly asked in MC format.

label: Reading
text: Multiple-choice questions

label: Reading
text: Read the question and study all the options first carefully. Try to make predictions about which options are possible answers and which can be eliminated straightaway.

label: Reading
text: Skim the title, subtitle, the first and last paragraphs as well as the first and the last sentences of the other paragraphs to find the part of the text that is related to the question.

label: Reading
text: Understanding the writer's purpose

label: Reading
text: You have learnt how to use skimming to get an idea of the general theme or gist of a text. Once you understand the theme of a text, you can probably identify its purpose. Texts are written for many different purposes, such as:

label: Reading
text: to argue

label: Reading
text: to criticize

label: Reading
text: to entertain

label: Reading
text: to evaluate

label: Reading
text: to explore

label: Reading
text: to express

label: Reading
text: to inform (provide information)

label: Reading
text: to instruct (teach)

label: Reading
text: to persuade

label: Reading
text: to satirize (show that someone/something is wrong, similar to criticize)

label: Reading
text: The first five wordings are mainly for challenging someone/something.

label: Reading
text: Please be reminded that a text may also have more than one intended purpose.

label: Reading
text: Skill 1: Copy or don't copy?

label: Reading
text: Copy if the question is in the format of "according to...", "based on..." or "using the info...".

label: Reading
text: DO NOT copy if the question is in the format of "imply...".

label: Reading
text: Skill 2: Find the clue

label: Reading
text: The question keyword(s) can be found in the passage.

label: Reading
text: Synonym(s) of the question keyword(s) can be found in the passage.

label: Reading
text: Identify if the question is positive or negative, then look for positive/negative elements in the passage.

label: Reading
text: Skill 3: Look forwards or backwards?

label: Reading
text: effect because cause

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: something can cause

label: Reading
text: Skill 4: Reference Questions

label: Reading
text: Reference questions are in the format of "... replace ..." or "... refer to ...".

label: Reading
text: This is an existing concept - the answer is usually found by looking backwards at the sentence(s) before the referenced word.

label: Reading
text: Skill 5: Spot the "Two"

label: Reading
text: Pay attention to prefixes, "and", "with", "duo", "both", "pair".

label: Reading
text: Prefixes that signal "two" or "together":

label: Reading
text: bi- (bicycle, bilingual, bilateral)

label: Reading
text: di- (dichotomy, dioxide)

label: Reading
text: duo- (duopoly, duologue)

label: Reading
text: twi- (twin, twilight)

label: Reading
text: ambi- (ambidextrous - using both hands)

label: Reading
text: amphi- (amphibian - living in both water and land)

label: Reading
text: co- (cooperate, coexist - together)

label: Reading
text: syn-/sym- (synergy, symphony - together)

label: Reading
text: inter- (interact, interconnect - between)

label: Reading
text: Why this is crucial:

label: Reading
text: When a question contains these signals, the answer almost always requires TWO elements, not one. For example, if the question asks about a "pair" of reasons or uses "both", you must find two answers in the passage. Students who miss this signal often give only one answer and lose marks. Spotting the "two" signal early tells you exactly how many points to look for.

text: Question: According to Pat, why do parents want to keep their children away from the TV and computer?

label: Reading
text: Skill 1:

label: Reading
text: The question is in the format of "according to...", so our answer should be copied from the passage.

label: Reading

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: We can see the exact keywords at the start of paragraph 2, in the sentence 'Parents want pastimes that will keep their children away from the TV and computer'.

label: Reading

label: Reading

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: Example 2 2017 DSE P1 A Q07

label: Reading
text: Recycling has been relentlessly promoted as a goal in and of itself: a public and private virtue that is indoctrinated in students from kindergarten through university. As a result, otherwise well-informed and educated people have no idea of the relative costs and benefits.

label: Reading
text: Question: According to the passage, why are people ill-informed about recycling?

label: Reading
text: The question is in the format of 'according to...', so our answer should be copied from the passage.

label: Reading
text: Question keyword: ill-informed

label: Reading
text: The ending sentence of the paragraph 'otherwise well-informed and educated people have no idea of the relative costs and benefits' implies that people are 'ill-informed about recycling'.

label: Reading
text: Some students may not know the word 'ill-informed'. There is another way to solve the problem:

label: Reading
text: We know that the word 'ill-informed' is negative, 'have no idea' is also negative. Thus, we understand that 'ill-informed about recycling' and the ending sentence of the paragraph are connected.

label: Reading
text: In the beginning of the ending sentence of the paragraph, we can see 'As a result'. Therefore, the cause of people being 'ill-informed about recycling' is behind 'As a result'.

label: Reading
text: This is because a public and private virtue that is indoctrinated in students from kindergarten through university.

label: Reading
text: You started, like so many other Westerners in Korea, teaching English. When did you begin writing about Korea and why?

label: Reading

label: Reading

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: [6] Central to our stewardship program, however, is employee engagement. Last year, we had about 60 'Go Green Ambassadors' but less than 50 percent of our employees attended our sustainability events. We have three measures to improve employee engagement.

label: Reading

Additionally, we should provide rewards for different teams and departments when they meet their key performance indicators. Finally, we plan to host innovation contests for our employees to promote solutions that are unique and applicable to their specific departments.

text: Question: Complete the following summary by writing ONE word taken from paragraphs 6 to 7 in each blank below. Your answers must be grammatically correct. (4 marks)

label: Reading
text: The (i) ________ of our staff members is the key to our success in environmental goals. For this reason, we would like to implement three initiatives that aim to increase participation. To raise their awareness of all Star Resort environmental policies, (ii) ________ will be mandatory for all new employees. We know that all employees like to receive (iii) ________ when they reach their targets. So these will be provided as our second initiative. Also, employee ownership of initiatives is a motivator so we can hold competitions to encourage employees' (iv) ________ in finding new solutions.

text: Skill 0: Analyze the constraints (Basic Skill)

label: Reading
text: Before reading the passage, note the constraints from the question:

label: Reading
text: Quantity: ONE word per blank.

label: Reading
text: Source: Taken from paragraphs 6 to 7 (the answer must be found here).

label: Reading
text: Requirement: Answers must be grammatically correct.

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: (i) The ________ of our staff members is the key to our success...

label: Reading
text: Clue: "staff members" is a synonym for "employees". "Key to our success" relates to being "Central to our stewardship program".

label: Reading
text: Location: Paragraph 6, first sentence: "Central to our stewardship program, however, is employee engagement."

label: Reading

label: Reading
text: (ii) To raise their awareness of all Star Resort environmental policies, ________ will be mandatory for all new employees.

label: Reading
text: Clue: "raise their awareness" is a synonym for "increase awareness". "mandatory for all new employees" matches "All new staff need to attend".

label: Reading
text: Location: Paragraph 7, first sentence: "All new staff need to attend training sessions to increase awareness..."

label: Reading
text: Answer: training (Note: We choose "training" instead of "training sessions" because the question requires ONE word).

label: Reading
text: (iii) We know that all employees like to receive ________ when they reach their targets.

label: Reading
text: Clue: "reach their targets" is a synonym for "meet their key performance indicators". "receive" relates to "provide".

label: Reading
text: Location: Paragraph 7, second sentence: "Additionally, we should provide rewards for different teams and departments when they meet their key performance indicators."

label: Reading
text: Answer: rewards.

label: Reading
text: (iv) ...hold competitions to encourage employees' ________ in finding new solutions.

label: Reading
text: Clue: "competitions" relates to "contests". "encourage employees'" relates to "for our employees to promote".

label: Reading
text: Location: Paragraph 7, third sentence: "Finally, we plan to host innovation contests for our employees to promote solutions..."

label: Reading
text: Answer: innovation.

label: Speaking
text: Group Discussion

label: Speaking
text: Preparation for Discussion

label: Speaking
text: The mastery of several language skills is required to do a good discussion. The skills below will deal with preparation work. In fact, preparation for discussion both orally or in the form of a writing is an on-going process. Students should be reading widely and regularly so as to be able to contribute meaningfully to a discussion on any topics including social issues. It has frequently been remarked in HKEAA Examination Reports that candidates generally perform better if the themes of the passages are related to their daily lives especially those about school matters. It is also suggested that students should expose themselves to the world around them. Reading newspapers, journals and magazines regularly, attending live forums or watching the broadcast on television, browing websites for articles or speeches on hot topics can all help to widen students' knowledge of the bigger world.

label: Speaking
text: Understanding the Passage

label: Speaking
text: Students should read the passage most carefully to understand:

label: Speaking
text: the theme of the passage

label: Speaking
text: the genre of the passage

label: Speaking
text: the discussion task(s)

label: Speaking
text: the suggested points for discussion

label: Speaking
text: The discussion task usually comprises two parts, first, discussing the topic itself; second, deciding how to present the points discussed for a specific purpose as in writing a complaint letter, writing an article or preparing a presentation. However, students should not just limit themselves to the suggested points when doing the discussion.

label: Speaking
text: Managing the Discussion

label: Speaking
text: If time is running out and the other students are still talking about the same point, do not try to interrupt them awkardly. Instead, express your opinions regarding to the students' points, and do your best to bridge the conversation from the current point to the next point.

label: Speaking
text: Comprehending the Passage

label: Speaking
text: You should first read the title. It might be the summary of the whole passage. It might be a question to raise a query.

label: Speaking
text: You should also note the type and genre of the passage. The passage can be any kind of text. This can help you to understand the tone faster.

label: Speaking
text: If you discover that there are wrods you don't understand, try to guess. Don't just skip them.

label: Speaking
text: If you discover words you can't pronounce, decide if they are crucial. See if you can substitute. If you can't, then try to say those words several times until you are in control of the pronunciation. Don't be scared and panic by words that you can't pronounce.

label: Speaking
text: Taking Notes

label: Speaking
text: IMPORTANT: Your notes must be neat and tidy for easy reading. Don't scribble.

label: Speaking
text: You are to write down only the main ideas of the passage. Not all names and figures are important.

label: Speaking
text: You might make your notes in the form of bullet points, a mind-map or a flow-chart. You can use symbols and abbreviations. Please DO NOT write out a whole essay or copy the whole passage for presentation.

label: Speaking
text: You can pratice all forms of note-taking. Reflect on how useful your notes are every time you do your practice. Find out the kind of notes that can help you most.

label: Speaking
text: You are also to note down your own ideas regarding the topic. Be original and creative but practical. Don't be over-creative. Taking your role seriously can help you.

text: Model Essay (943 words):

label: Writing
text: Group work acts as an indispensable method of gathering ideas from diversified colleagues, with their minds brimming with distinct thoughts and opinions, it has long been acknowledged as a conducive way of contributing information and ideas to the workplace. Yet the efficiency of groupwork has become contentious as workers are plagued by the challenges of working with others in their team. What are the challenges of group work that has arose lately in the workplace? This essay will underscore three pivotal challenges and provide corresponding solutions.

label: Writing
text: First and foremost, group work encompasses unequal distribution of duties to the workers. Nowadays, we are no stranger to the terms "slackers" and "free-riders" which indicate those who contribute minimal work to their assigned tasks and those who highly depend on their groupmates on producing quality work. These workers also prowl in the workplace, unleashing their laziness and irresponsibility to their unsuspecting colleagues. This is substantiated by a report from the University of Michigan, which conducted a survey on American employees and the results show a staggering 80% of employees having to confront "slackers" and "free-riders" during group work in the office. It also stated that respondents feel dissatisfied, incensed and frustrated when it comes to encountering such incompetent colleagues in the workplace. "Never again, would I volunteer to be in a team project," asserted Mr Smith who worked in the large conglomerate - United Projects, which is renowned for operating team projects on scientific research. "It is nice to collect different opinions from my fellow colleagues, but I could spare those who bask in the praise and accolade from the leaders when they contributed nothing to the project," he exclaimed. It is no doubt a headache for diligent workers who aspire all colleagues to work wholeheartedly on the project, and when a worker is inundated with the tasks of a teammate who is not willing to contribute, it can be seen that group work may pose as a challenge and become unfavourable to workers.

label: Writing
text: Additionally, group work amasses a myriad of opinions, and when colleagues uphold different stances, relationships could be a trouble to maintain. A syndicate of workers though with the same objective, may hold contrasting visions to execute a plan. Ms Young, an acclaimed marine scientist of the famous "Bring Our Freshwater Turtles Back to Shore" conservation program grimly accounted the brainstorming process of their research: "There was a variety of ideas on how we could kickstart our research; some suggested a field research, some suggested a research on only bringing turtles in captive back to the wild. We had limited time to work on the project and it was disastrous when we couldn't reach a consensus and make ends meet. Incompatibility in group work is really the worst thing." These heated arguments proved deleterious to office relationships as workers hold dissatisfaction, annoyance and frustration towards their counterparts, resulting in infeasible work performance and outcome. A questionnaire published by government investigation company Joy in Office, Inc., counted over 15,000 failed team projects amongst outstanding commercial companies, with 85% of the failed attempts owing to incompatibility amongst groupmates. This implies that tense work relationships resulted by group work in the office acts as a hindrance to the performance of companies. With incompatibility being a major factor to dissatisfaction in the workplace, it can be seen why group work remains a challenge to workers and they are hesitant to participate in more team projects.

label: Writing
text: Last but not least, group work could be inflexible to workers and hinders them from working to the best of their ability. As employees come together to discuss on their group work, meetings, documents, communication methods have to be agreed on unanimously to ensure efficiency. A survey conducted by Harvard University states that inflexibility is the main contributer to the unpopularity of group work in the workplace in 2024. "As the digital world becomes more pervasive, people tend to think that they can work efficiently despite geographical boundaries through online means. Though a laudable attempt, the effort to group a number of workers to meet up on a certain date, at a certain time, in different places is an exorbitant labour to some." Mr Smith, a sociology professor from Harvard University contends. A natural phenomenon observed nowadays would be that people would like to work in a flexible way, whenever and wherever they want, and with group work, it is hard to do that. It is seen that group work is a less prominent option for workers as they want to work faster and more efficiently with technology; group work requires too much planning and is not worth the wait to work any more.

label: Writing
text: Despite the challenges of group work in the workplace, there are a few ways to simply tackle the difficulties. Firstly, by creating task lists and requiring workers to state the person-in-charge of each assigned part of duty. It can eliminate the risk of prospective "slackers" and "free-riders" from emerging, as they need to harbour the responsibility of a part that everyone knows that they need to take part in.

label: Writing
text: Secondly, workers can make use of online resources such as polls and brainstorming websites to overlook all the workers' opinions. These resources offer anonymous identities for workers to voice out their opinions without the fear of being overlooked or not considered. These techniques help in ensuring just and fair treatment to all opinions and ideas can be presented in a more clear way to reduce hostility in critical opinions.

label: Writing
text: In conclusion, there are challenges to group work but by attempting these alternative solutions in team projects, group work in the office may be milder and more just and collaborative!

text: Model Essay: Letter of Advice — Sibling Jealousy

label: Writing
text: Model Letter:

label: Writing
text: Hello Philip,

label: Writing
text: Living together with your family can be a wonderful experience but it also leads to various kinds of problems. Brothers and sisters are often compared to each other, and while that can be positive, it can also be challenging at times. Since your sister is very successful in different sports, it is no surprise that she gets praise from lots of different people.

label: Writing
text: Feelings of jealousy about a more successful sibling are natural. When we hear our brother or sister being praised by friends or family, it is difficult not to compare ourselves to them and think about the fact that we are not the ones being told how wonderful we are. As a result, this can knock our confidence. Don't feel guilty about your jealousy. You should focus instead on ways to make yourself feel stronger and happier.

label: Writing
text: Moreover, I would suggest that you use your jealousy of your sister to motivate yourself to find your own things to be successful at. It may be that you are never going to be great at sports, but if you examine your own life or experiment with new things, you will find your own niche - the thing that you can do better than your sister. Have you thought about joining a school club? You may find something you can enjoy and become skilled in.

label: Writing
text: What's more, I would say that you should also learn to praise your sister. This might sound contradictory to the idea of feeling better about yourself. However, praise is a generous act; and if you can praise your sister, you will feel better about yourself too - kind acts generally make us feel better about ourselves!

label: Writing
text: My advice to you is to learn to accept your jealousy. Use it as a means of increasing your drive and ambition to be successful at your own special talent. I'm sure that if you work hard towards your target, you will forget about your jealousy and perhaps learn to share your passion with your sister and the rest of your family.

label: Writing
text: Best wishes,Andrew

label: Writing
text: Structure of the Letter:

label: Writing
text: Informal salutation: Other common salutations include Hi or Dear + the recipient's first name.

label: Writing
text: Opening paragraph: Keep it short. Try to show that you understand the recipient's problem and how he/she feels.

label: Writing
text: Body paragraphs: Each paragraph should contain one main idea. Group related suggestions and advice into paragraphs.

label: Writing
text: Closing paragraph: Summarize your suggestions and encourage the recipient to try them out.

label: Writing
text: Friendly closing: Other friendly closings include Cheers, All the best and Best regards.

label: Writing
text: Modal Verbs in the Letter:

label: Writing
text: Modal verbs such as should and would are used throughout the letter. They soften the advice so that it sounds like gentle guidance rather than a command, which keeps the tone polite and persuasive — exactly what a letter of advice needs.

label: Writing
text: "You should focus instead on ways to make yourself feel stronger and happier." — paragraph 2

label: Writing
text: "Moreover, I would suggest that you use your jealousy of your sister to motivate yourself..." — paragraph 3

label: Writing

label: Writing
text: First Conditional in the Letter:

label: Writing
text: The first conditional (if + present simple, will + base verb) is used throughout the letter to elaborate possible scenarios — it shows the recipient what good things will happen if he follows the advice. This makes the advice feel concrete, achievable and encouraging.

text: The 57 Bus

label: Recommendations
text: by Dashka Slater

label: Recommendations
text: The 57 Bus is a work of nonfiction by journalist Dashka Slater, published in 2017. It's written for a young adult audience but has been widely read by adults as well, and won several awards, including a Stonewall Book Award.

label: Recommendations
text: The book tells the true story of an incident that occurred in Oakland, California, in 2013, involving two teenagers who rode the same city bus line — the 57 — but attended different high schools and moved in very different social worlds.

label: Recommendations
text: Sasha was a white, agender teen (using they/them pronouns) attending a private school, known for being intellectually curious, into linguistics and math, and part of a close-knit, supportive friend group.

label: Recommendations
text: Richard was a Black teen from a low-income East Oakland neighborhood, attending a public school, trying to stay out of trouble and build a better future for himself and his family.

label: Recommendations
text: One afternoon, as a prank, Richard set fire to the skirt Sasha was wearing while they slept on the bus, causing severe burns. The incident led to Richard being charged as an adult with a hate crime, sparking intense media attention and forcing both communities to grapple with questions of race, class, gender identity, juvenile justice, and the consequences of a split-second decision.

label: Recommendations
text: Slater's reporting is notably even-handed — she doesn't flatten either teenager into a simple villain or victim, instead exploring:

label: Recommendations
text: Gender identity — an accessible explanation of what it means to be agender/nonbinary, and Sasha's journey of understanding their own identity

label: Recommendations
text: Racial and economic disparity — how Richard's background and the justice system's treatment of Black youth shaped the case's outcome

label: Recommendations
text: The juvenile justice system — questions about whether trying teenagers as adults, and hate crime enhancements, serve justice or simply punishment

label: Recommendations
text: Empathy and complexity — the book resists easy narratives, asking readers to hold compassion for both teens simultaneously

label: Recommendations
text: The book is structured almost like an extended piece of long-form journalism, moving between Sasha's and Richard's perspectives and weighing in courtroom proceedings, interviews, and social context.

label: Recommendations
text: It's frequently used in classrooms and book clubs as a way to open discussions about identity, restorative justice, and unconscious bias, and is generally recommended to readers interested in social-justice-oriented nonfiction or true stories that resist tidy moral conclusions.

text: The Perks of Being a Wallflower

label: Recommendations
text: by Stephen Chbosky

label: Recommendations
text: The Perks of Being a Wallflower is a coming-of-age epistolary novel by Stephen Chbosky, published in 1999. It's written as a series of letters from the protagonist to an anonymous, unnamed recipient — addressed only as "Dear friend" — which gives the book an intimate, diary-like quality.

label: Recommendations
text: The story follows Charlie, an introverted, sensitive high school freshman in the early 1990s near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Charlie is still reeling from the recent suicide of his best friend and the earlier death of his beloved aunt Helen, and he struggles to navigate the social world of high school. Over the course of his freshman year, he's taken under the wing of two seniors, stepsiblings Sam and Patrick, who introduce him to their circle of friends, first loves, music, and the world of "participating" in life rather than just observing it.

label: Recommendations
text: Through his letters, Charlie writes candidly about:

label: Recommendations
text: First experiences — first parties, first relationships, first exposure to drugs and alcohol

label: Recommendations
text: Mental health — the novel deals openly with depression, trauma, and Charlie's own psychological struggles, building toward a revelation about his past late in the book

label: Recommendations
text: Sexuality and identity — including Patrick's experience as a gay teen in a less accepting era

label: Recommendations
text: Family dynamics and loss — grief, complicated family relationships, and the search for belonging

label: Recommendations
text: The pain and beauty of adolescence — the book is often remembered for its bittersweet, aching tone about the fleeting nature of youth

label: Recommendations
text: The novel became something of a touchstone for a generation of teen readers, prized for its honest, unfiltered portrayal of subjects that were often sanitized in young adult fiction at the time. Its frank treatment of drug use, sexuality, and abuse has also made it one of the more frequently challenged or banned books in American schools and libraries.

label: Recommendations
text: Chbosky wrote and directed the 2012 film adaptation himself, starring Logan Lerman, Emma Watson, and Ezra Miller, which is generally regarded as a faithful and well-received translation of the book.

label: Recommendations
text: It's often recommended to readers who enjoy character-driven, emotionally raw coming-of-age stories — though given its content, it tends to resonate most with older teens and adults rather than younger readers.

text: If you or someone you know is struggling with thoughts of suicide, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988 in the US) is available 24/7.

text: Becoming

label: Recommendations
text: by Michelle Obama

label: Recommendations
text: Becoming is the memoir of Michelle Obama, published in November 2018. It became a massive bestseller, selling over 10 million copies in its first year and being translated into more than 30 languages — one of the best-selling memoirs of all time.

label: Recommendations
text: The book is structured in three parts, tracing her life chronologically:

label: Recommendations
text: "Becoming Me" — Her childhood on the South Side of Chicago in a working-class Black family, her education at Princeton and Harvard Law School, and the beginnings of her legal career.

label: Recommendations
text: "Becoming Us" — Meeting and marrying Barack Obama, her career transition into public service and nonprofit work, balancing motherhood with her professional life, and the grueling experience of his early political campaigns, including the 2008 presidential run.

label: Recommendations
text: "Becoming More" — Her eight years as First Lady, covering initiatives like Let's Move! and Let Girls Learn, life inside the White House with her daughters, and the challenges of being one of the most scrutinized women in the world — including candid reflections on race, public image, and the pressures placed on her family.

label: Recommendations
text: What distinguishes Becoming from a typical political memoir is its intimacy and voice. Obama writes in a warm, conversational style and is notably candid about personal struggles — including a miscarriage, using IVF to conceive her daughters, and going to couples counseling with Barack during a difficult stretch of their marriage. She also reflects frankly on navigating racism and sexism, both before and during her time in the White House.

label: Recommendations
text: Thematically, the book centers on identity and self-invention — the idea that "becoming" is an ongoing process rather than a fixed achievement, a message that resonated widely with readers regardless of political affiliation, and helped the book cross into a broader cultural phenomenon (including a Netflix documentary and a companion journal).

label: Recommendations
text: It's often recommended to readers interested in memoir, women's leadership, or American political history, though it stays more personal than policy-focused — readers looking for a deep dive into Obama-era politics may find it leans more toward the emotional and biographical.

text: The Alchemist

label: Recommendations
text: by Paulo Coelho

label: Recommendations
text: The Alchemist by Paulo Coelho is a short, fable-like novel first published in Portuguese in 1988. It's become one of the best-selling books in history, translated into dozens of languages.

label: Recommendations
text: The story follows Santiago, a young Andalusian shepherd who dreams repeatedly of finding treasure at the Egyptian pyramids. After consulting a fortune-teller and a mysterious old king named Melchizedek, he sells his flock and sets out on a journey across North Africa to pursue this "Personal Legend" — Coelho's term for one's true calling or life purpose.

label: Recommendations
text: Along the way, Santiago meets a series of guides and obstacles: a con man who robs him, a crystal merchant he works for in Tangier, an Englishman studying alchemy, and, most significantly, Fatima, a woman he falls in love with at an oasis, and an alchemist who becomes his mentor and teaches him to listen to his heart and read the omens of the desert.

label: Recommendations
text: The novel is really a philosophical parable dressed as an adventure story. Its central themes include:

label: Recommendations
text: Following your dreams — the idea that the universe conspires to help those pursuing their true purpose

label: Recommendations
text: The journey over the destination — treasure, in the end, isn't quite what Santiago expects

label: Recommendations
text: Listening to intuition — Coelho frames the "heart" and natural signs as sources of wisdom

label: Recommendations
text: Alchemy as metaphor — transforming base metal into gold mirrors the process of self-realization

label: Recommendations
text: Coelho writes in simple, accessible prose, which is part of why the book has resonated with such a broad international audience — though that same simplicity has also drawn criticism from some readers who find its aphorisms ("when you want something, all the universe conspires in helping you to achieve it") a bit too tidy or sentimental.

label: Recommendations
text: It's often recommended as a quick, reflective read for anyone at a crossroads or thinking about purpose and risk-taking, though whether its optimism feels inspiring or a little glib tends to depend a lot on the reader.

text: Sharma positions himself as a mentor figure throughout — the book draws on his experience having mentored billionaires, superstar athletes, and heads of state, teaching them this same framework.

text: In terms of reception, reader reviews are mixed but generally positive. Some found it repetitive of his earlier work or noted that anecdotes could feel disconnected from the surrounding material, making parts of the book feel inconsistent, while others considered it an important read offering a refreshing perspective in a society obsessed with material success.

label: Recommendations
text: It's best suited to readers who enjoy Sharma's aphoristic, motivational style (fans of The 5AM Club will find it familiar territory) and who want a framework for thinking about success more holistically — though like much of the genre, it leans more on inspiration and repeated principles than on rigorous evidence.
